people that walk with their heads downwards! The antipathies, I think—” (she was rather glad there was no one listening, this time,
as it didn’t sound at all the right word) “—but I shall have to ask them what the name of the country is, you know. Please, Ma’am, is

think you could manage it?) “And what an ignorant little girl she’ll think me for asking! No, it’ll never do to ask: perhaps I shall see it written up somewhere.”

think!” (Dinah was the cat.) “I hope they’ll remember her saucer of milk at tea-time. Dinah, my dear! I wish you were down here with
me! There are no mice in the air, I’m afraid, but you might catch a bat, and that’s very like a mouse, you know. But do cats eat bats,
I wonder?” And here Alice began to get rather sleepy, and went on saying to herself, in a dreamy sort of way, “Do cats eat bats? Do
cats eat bats?” and sometimes “Do bats eat cats?”, for, you see, as she couldn’t answer either question, it didn’t much matter which
way she put it. She felt that she was dozing off, and had just begun to dream that she was walking hand in hand with Dinah, and
was saying to her, very earnestly, “Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?” when suddenly, thump! thump! down she came
upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall was over.
Alice was not a bit hurt, and she jumped up on to her feet in a moment: she looked up, but it was all dark overhead: before her was
another long passage, and the White Rabbit was still in sight, hurrying down it.

get-childitem -r -attributes !directory -path test_input | % {$_.fullname} | foreach-object { & "wkhtmltopdf.exe" -O landscape --enable-local-file-access $_ "test_output\\$_.pdf" }

If, instead of length I use namestring:

get-childitem -r -attributes !directory -path test_input | % {$_.fullname} | foreach-object { & "wkhtmltopdf.exe" -O landscape --enable-local-file-access $_ "test_output\\$($_.namestring).pdf" }

I'm working on a proprietary font that uses custom glyphs for certain units of measure. For example, I want to display pH for acidity as a single glyph, or nm for nanometers, etc. This font is primarily for use in a program I'm developing, but I would like the text to be as portable as possible. This is my first foray into Unicode, or really anything like this, and I'm struggling with how best to accomplish my goal.

My first thought was to stick the custom glyphs in one of the Private Use Areas, but these encodings are non-portable. Any text copied from my program into another one without the proper font installed would show a generic "unknown" glyph or something similar. I'd prefer the "pH" codepoint to be decomposed into an ASCII "p" and "H" in this case, but PUA codes are specifically ignored during normalization to ensure round-trip fidelity.

I did find some of the symbols I'm looking for, such as 33D7 SQUARE PH and 339A SQUARE NM, but not all of the ones I'll need. SQUARE PH in particular has a casing "anomaly" in the decomposition, which is annoying. These are also in the CJK compatibility section, which makes me wonder if they're intended for general use or East Asian scripts specifically.

I have also looked at Variation Selectors, since they have the desirable property that they can be ignored when unsupported. From what I understand these are limited to a specific set (actually 3 specific sets) of Unicode-blessed variations, and are not generally extensible.

It also occurred to me that this problem could almost be described as providing a custom ligature. Like replacing ff or fi; except in my case it's pH, nm, and others. But from what I can tell, ligatures are assigned official codepoints, and I haven't found a mechanism for adding non-standard or provisional extensions. This is also slightly different, because I want the replacement to be based on context. I don't want the nm in "unmet" to use the custom "nm" glyph, for example. (To be clear, I'm not expecting my program to automatically determine when the substitution is appropriate. I understand and expect that I'll have to encode the context into the text somehow.)

Does anyone have any input on how I might accomplish this? To summarize, the problem statement is that I'd like to provide custom glyphs for particular multi-character units of measure, and I would like the text to be portable to systems that do not have my custom font installed.

My question could apply to many other ruby frameworks I guess. But here I have the case while programming a Jekyll project.

Let's see this Jekyll plugin as an example:

require 'dotenv'


module Jekyll
  class EnvironmentVariablesGenerator < Generator
    priority :highest

    def generate(site)
      site.config['env'] = Dotenv.load
      Jekyll.logger.debug "#{__FILE__} Loading env variables: "
      Jekyll.logger.debug site.config.to_yaml
    end
  end

end

Why is Jekyll.logger magically available? I've read the "Programming Ruby" book, and while it explains how require works when writing your own standalone program, it doesn't explain how a framework such as Jekyll makes things available in the scope of some ruby files. I find it quite confusing, being more used to ES6 that always as explicit imports.
